description:
We are a Surat-based team taking on the Dancing with the SARs challenge! Earth's surface is constantly shifting through floods, farming cycles, and coastal changes, and we want to build an interactive tool using NASA-ISRO NISAR radar data to make those patterns easy to see and understand.

What We Bring:
We currently handle core coding, data processing, and application logic.
summary:
We developed the Kaziranga Monsoon Water Observatory, an interactive web app backed by a reproducible Python pipeline. It tracks seasonal surface water and L-band radar response across Assam’s Kaziranga floodplain using 2026 NASA–ISRO NISAR L2 GCOV observations.

For the Dancing with the SARs challenge, we turn dual-polarization (HH and HV) radar data into something anyone can explore. Users step through 10 repeat acquisitions from June to October 2026, compare any date against an October 14 baseline with a swipe, and switch between four views: water-like extent, raw radar, how often each area was wet, and an experimental vegetation-change layer. Every area estimate includes a threshold-sensitivity range, and results can be downloaded as CSV.

This matters because monsoon cloud limits optical satellites exactly when water patterns matter most. By making NISAR data easier to read and stating the limits of radar interpretation, the observatory connects satellite observations with a clearer picture of seasonal change on a floodplain that supports wetlands, wildlife and nearby communities.
details:
Kaziranga Monsoon Water Observatory (https://github.com/Parth-Degharia09/kaziranga-sar-change-detector) is an interactive web app, backed by a reproducible Python pipeline, that shows how surface water and L-band radar response changed across Assam’s Kaziranga floodplain during the 2026 monsoon, using NASA–ISRO NISAR L2 GCOV data.

How it works. The pipeline reads 10 repeat Track 040 acquisitions (June–October 2026, HH and HV), averages speckle noise, converts to dB, and flags smooth water-like surfaces (HH below −15.5 dB). It exports map overlays and a metrics file for a static web app. Users swipe any date against an October 14 baseline and switch between four views: water-like extent, raw radar, how often each area was wet, and an experimental vegetation-change layer. We add NASA GPM IMERG rainfall, and users can download results as CSV.

Why it matters. Monsoon cloud often blinds optical satellites when flood information matters most. Radar sees through cloud. Our tool turns hard-to-read radar data into something anyone can explore, so people can see where water spreads across wetlands and wildlife habitat.

What we considered. We call results “water-like”, not “flood”, because rivers, wetlands, paddies and wet sandbars all look dark to radar. Every area includes a ±2 dB cutoff sensitivity range. We flag that the NISAR data is provisional and that no pass exists from 27 July to 10 August.

Tools. Python (NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image, rasterio, Matplotlib, Pillow), JavaScript, Leaflet, Chart.js, Tailwind CSS, GitHub Pages.

Creativity. A before/after swipe, a wetness-frequency map, an experimental HH/HV vegetation layer, and plain-language headlines with the limits stated up front.

SI use. We used Claude and Gemini for coding help, debugging, drafting documentation and slides. We ran and checked the pipeline and app ourselves.
